## CHAPTER 02
PREAMBLE, NATURE, PARTS & SCHEDULES

### THEME ANALYSIS
1. REPEATS

#### A. Preamble and its Keywords
- On 26 January 1950 India was a Sovereign Democratic Republic; Socialist and Secular came in 1976 [2021].
- Economic liberty is no Preamble objective; the Preamble mirrors the makers' mind [2017].
- It is part of the Constitution but has no independent legal effect [2020].

#### B. Parts, Schedules and Concluding Articles
- Part IXA municipalities, Part XVIII emergency, Part XX amendment [2024].
- Seventh Schedule traps: inter State quarantine is Union [2024]; education spans many provisions [2012].
- Eighth Schedule holds 22 languages [2024, 2008]; classical language status is separate [2015, 2014].

#### C. Ninth and Tenth Schedules
- The Ninth Schedule came with the First Amendment, 1951; entries after 1973 face Basic Structure review [2019,
2018].
- The Tenth Schedule carries anti defection [2014]; the presiding officer decides with no time frame [2022].
- Political party appears in the Constitution only through the Tenth Schedule [2025].

#### D. Basic Features and Core Concepts
- A Constitution defines and limits government power [2023, 2021, 2020, 2014].
- Rule of law: limitation of powers, equality before law, liberty and civil rights [2018].
- Separation of powers best safeguards liberty [2021]; due process means natural justice [2023].
- Concept staples: liberty [2019, 2018], rights against the State, equality as absence of privileges [2017].
2. HOW THE FORMAT HAS CHANGED
- 2008 to 2014: direct recall of Schedules, languages and anti defection [2008, 2012, 2014]
- 2017 to 2023: one best answer concept questions on liberty, rule of law, State and constitutional government [2017,
2019, 2021, 2023]
- 2024 to 2025: multi statement sets on Parts, Lists and ratification [2024, 2025]
- 2026: the "which conclusion is correct" format, judging three statements together [2026]
3. WHAT IS BEING ASKED NOW
- The bare text: which Part holds what [2024], subjects needing State ratification [2025], Articles that name the
Constitution, repeal the old Acts and fix commencement [2026]
- Tenth Schedule detail: who decides disqualification, and whether "political party" is mentioned [2025]
- One concept question per paper still appears [2023]

### [Prelims Source Page 19](pages/prelims/prelims_page_019.pdf)

Constitutional Supremacy
1. Proper synthesis between the British principle of Parliamentary sovereignty(Parliament has the sole authority over law
making on anything) and the
2. American principle of judicial supremacy(judiciary the ultimate authority to interpret the Constitution and laws of a
country.) In India we have Constitutional supremacy where the constitution is supreme not the organs.
Integrated + independent judiciary
1. SC at top of hierarchy then HC for one or more states below SC then below it subordinate courts.
2. Separation of powers under art 50 to keep judiciary independent.
Fundamental Rights
1. Six Fundamental Rights, in Part III (Arts 12 to 35).
2. Promote the ideal of political democracy.
3. Act as a limitation on the tyranny of the executive and on arbitrary laws of the legislature.
4. Justiciable and enforceable through Arts 32 and 226.
DPSPs
1. Contained in Part IV (Arts 36 to 51).
2. Promote the ideal of social and economic democracy.
3. Non justiciable under Art 37, yet declared fundamental in the governance of the country and a duty of the State to apply
in making laws.
Fundamental Duties
1. Ten Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh
Committee.
2. The eleventh, on providing education to a child between six and fourteen, was added by the 86th Amendment, 2002, so
there are eleven in all.
3. They sit in Part IVA, in the single Article 51A.
4. Not directly enforceable by any court, but given effect through ordinary statutes.
Secular State
Indian secularism means the State has no religion of its own and gives equal respect to all faiths, rather than the Western
wall of separation between religion and State.
It ensures
1. that one religious community does not dominate another;
2. that some members do not dominate other members of the same religious community;
3. that the State neither enforces any particular religion nor takes away the religious freedom of individuals.
The word secular was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, though the concept was always implicit in Arts
14 to 16 and 25 to 28.

### [Prelims Source Page 20](pages/prelims/prelims_page_020.pdf)

PREAMBLE
Introduction [PRELIMS 2021,2017]
1. Origin: The US Constitution was the first to begin with a Preamble.
2. Philosophy: Contains the philosophy and basic values of the Constitution; called its “identity card” (N.A. Palkhivala),
“soul” (Thakurdas Bhargava) and “horoscope” (K.M. Munshi).
3. Source: Based on Nehru’s Objectives Resolution, moved on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947.
4. Amendment: “Socialist,” “Secular” and “Integrity” added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, the only amendment so
far; their insertion was upheld by the SC in Balram Singh v Union of India (2024).
5. Source of authority: Declares the people of India as the source of authority of the Constitution; the Preamble itself
is neither a source of power to the legislature nor a limit on it.
6. Non-justiciable: Not enforceable in courts on its own; its ideals work through other provisions.
7. Interpretation: States the ideals and objectives, and helps interpret provisions where the text is ambiguous.
8. Aspirations: Reflects the aspirations of the people to be achieved.
Preamble: Keywords and Objectives [PRELIMS 2017]
Order of words: “Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic”. The original Preamble (adopted 26 November 1949)
read “Sovereign Democratic Republic”; Socialist, Secular and Integrity were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
1. Sovereign
- India is neither a dependency nor a dominion; internally supreme and externally free from foreign control.
Commonwealth or UN membership does not dilute it.
- Can acquire foreign territory; but ceding Indian territory needs a constitutional amendment (Art 368), not an
ordinary law under Art 3 (In re Berubari Union, 1960, advisory opinion). Eg. 9th Amendment, 1960 (Berubari); 100th
Amendment, 2015 (Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh).
2. Socialist (42nd Amendment, 1976)
- Democratic socialism: a mixed economy where public and private sectors coexist; not communistic socialism or
state ownership of everything. Aims at a welfare State through DPSPs, without abolishing private property.
- Dr Balram Singh v Union of India (25 November 2024): SC upheld the insertion of “socialist” and “secular”;
“socialist” means a welfare State and does not restrict economic policy.
3. Secular (42nd Amendment, 1976)
- The idea already existed in Arts 14 to 16 and 25 to 28.
- No State religion; the State neither favours nor penalises any faith.
- Positive secularism: equal respect for all religions (sarva dharma sambhava), not the Western “wall of separation”.
- Part of the Basic Structure (S.R. Bommai, 1994).
4. Democratic
- Popular sovereignty: “We, the People of India” are the source of authority.
- Indirect (representative) parliamentary democracy, not direct democracy; referendum, initiative and recall are not
part of the constitutional scheme.
- Pillars:
- Universal adult franchise (Art 326; voting age lowered from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment, 1988)
- Periodic free and fair elections
- One person, one vote
- An independent judiciary and rule of law
- Aims at political, social and economic democracy, echoing Ambedkar’s warning about a “life of contradictions”.
5. Republic
- Head of State is elected, not hereditary: the President is indirectly elected for a fixed 5 year term (Arts 52, 54, 55),
unlike the British Crown.
- Political sovereignty rests with the people; no privileged class; all public offices open to every citizen without
discrimination.

### [Prelims Source Page 21](pages/prelims/prelims_page_021.pdf)

Objectives: Justice is taken from the Russian Revolution (1917); Liberty, Equality and Fraternity from the French Revolution
(1789).
6. Justice: Social, Economic, Political
- Social justice: no discrimination on grounds of caste, religion, sex etc. (Arts 15, 16, 17, 46).
- Economic justice: removal of gross inequalities in wealth and income (Arts 38, 39).
- Political justice: equal political rights and equal access to public office.
- Secured through a mix of Fundamental Rights and DPSPs.
7. Liberty: of Thought, Expression, Belief, Faith and Worship
- The Preamble secures only these five liberties; not “action” or “conscience”.
- Means absence of arbitrary restraint plus conditions for full development of personality.
- Not absolute: Art 19 rights are subject to reasonable restrictions.
8. Equality: of Status and Opportunity
- Core idea: absence of special privileges.
- Civic: Arts 14 to 18. Political: Arts 325, 326. Economic: Art 39(d) (equal pay for equal work).
9. Fraternity
- A sense of common brotherhood, promoted through single citizenship.
- Assures both (i) dignity of the individual and (ii) unity and integrity of the Nation; “Integrity” added in 1976.
- Reinforced by Fundamental Duty Art 51A(e).
Traps
- Word order: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.
- Justice from the Russian Revolution; Liberty, Equality, Fraternity from the French Revolution.
- Fraternity covers both dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the Nation.
- Liberty lists five items only; action and conscience are not among them.

Constitution and Constitutional Government [PRELIMS 2023,2021,2020,2014]
1. A Constitution is the fundamental law that constitutes the organs of government and allocates power among them, but

2. Constitutional government therefore means limited government - a government bound by the terms of the

in the interest of State authority.

(a) Justiciable Fundamental Rights (Part III), enforceable under Arts 32 and 226.

Due Process of Law vs Procedure Established by Law [PRELIMS 2023]
1. Article 21 as drafted adopted the 'procedure established by law' formula (traced to the Japanese Constitution): the
court asks only whether a competent legislature validly enacted the law and whether its procedure was followed.
2. 'Due process of law' (US 5th and 14th Amendments) goes further and requires the law and its procedure to be fair, just
and reasonable - in essence it embodies the principles of natural justice (nemo judex in causa sua - no one a judge in his
own cause; audi alteram partem - hear the other side).
3. In A.K. Gopalan v State of Madras (1950) the Supreme Court read Art 21 literally;
4. In Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978) it held that the procedure under Art 21 must be 'right, just and fair and not
arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive', effectively reading due process into the Constitution.
State, Government, Democracy and Bureaucracy [PRELIMS 2021,2020,2017]
1. In political theory the State has four essential elements - population, a definite territory, a government, and
sovereignty (independence of external control). Hence the correct definition is a community of persons permanently
occupying a definite territory, independent of external control and possessing an organised government;
2. long residence, common culture or tradition make a nation or a society, not a State.
3. The State is permanent and wider;
4. The government is only its agency and changes.
5. (Note: Art 12 gives a separate and wider working definition of 'the State' for the purposes of Part III.) Democracy's
superior virtue is that it calls into activity the intelligence and character of ordinary men and women, resting on
participation, accountability and universal adult franchise rather than on a single dynamic leader.
6. The bureaucracy is the permanent, politically neutral civil service whose characteristic function is the implementation of
public policy framed by the political executive;
7. Art 311 safeguards and the All India Services underpin it.
Rule of Law and Separation of Powers [PRELIMS 2021,2018]
1. Rule of Law comes from Britain and was explained by A.V. Dicey. It has three parts:
(a) Supremacy of law: no arbitrary power; the powers of government are limited.
(b) Equality before law: embodied in Art 14.
(c) Predominance of legal spirit: ordinary courts protect liberty and civil rights.
2. It does not include any 'responsibility of the people to the government';
3. The direction of accountability runs the other way.
4. The Rule of Law is part of the Basic Structure (Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain, 1975).
5. Separation of powers - the organic and functional distribution of authority among the legislature, executive and judiciary
with checks and balances - is regarded as the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy because it prevents
concentration of power;
6. India follows it functionally rather than absolutely (Art 50 separates the judiciary from the executive), and it too is part of
the Basic Structure.
Citizenship (Part II, Articles 5-11) [PRELIMS 2021]
1. India has single citizenship and a single domicile - there is no separate State citizenship, unlike the USA.
2. Arts 5-11 (Part II) deal only with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution;
3. Art 11 empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship by law, under which the Citizenship Act, 1955 was enacted.
4. It provides five modes of acquisition - birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory - and
three modes of loss - renunciation, termination and deprivation.
5. The Central Government can deprive a registered or naturalised citizen of citizenship if the person:
(a) obtained it by fraud;
(b) showed disloyalty to the Constitution;
(c) traded or communicated with the enemy during a war;
(d) was sentenced to two years' imprisonment within five years of registration or naturalisation;
(e) lived outside India for seven years continuously.
So citizenship, once granted, is not indefeasible.

Liberty, Equality, Rights and Social Capital [PRELIMS 2019,2018,2017]
1. Liberty is not mere absence of restraint or the opportunity to do whatever one likes;
2. in its positive sense it is the opportunity to develop oneself fully.
3. Law and liberty are complementary, not opposed - 'where there is no law there is no liberty' (John Locke) - because law

Constitutionalism and Constitutional Morality
1. Constitutionalism is the doctrine that governmental power must be limited by and exercised through law - 'limited
government'.
2. A country may possess a Constitution without having constitutionalism (authoritarian regimes have written
constitutions but unchecked power);
3. the two are therefore not the same thing.
4. Its essential ingredients are: rule of law, separation of powers with checks and balances, judicial review, enforceable
fundamental rights, an independent judiciary, free and fair periodic elections, and a government accountable to the
people.
5. Constitutional morality: a phrase Ambedkar borrowed from the historian George Grote and pressed in the Constituent
Assembly (4 November 1948).
It means following the spirit and core values of the Constitution, not mere literal legality, and the willingness of all actors
to work it with restraint.
6. Illustrations: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) - the proclamation dissolving the Bihar Assembly on the

7. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) - judicial review is part of the Basic Structure, so even Ninth Schedule laws

Sovereignty and its Kinds
Sovereignty is the supreme, original and independent authority of the State, one of the four essential elements of a State
and the one that distinguishes a State from every other association.
KINDS OF SOVEREIGNTY
1. Internal: supremacy over all persons and associations within the territory.
2. External: freedom from foreign control in the conduct of relations with other States.
3. Legal: the authority that makes law and whose commands the courts enforce. In India the Constitution is supreme; in
Britain, Parliament.
4. Political: the electorate behind the legal sovereign, whose will ultimately prevails.
5. Popular: power flows from the people, declared in the opening words WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA and worked through
universal adult franchise.
6. De jure against de facto: legal title to rule as against actual effective control.
7. Pluralist view (Harold Laski): the State is only one association among many and not absolutely supreme.
- Parliamentary sovereignty in the United Kingdom means no court can question an Act of Parliament.
- India instead follows constitutional supremacy, so Parliament's power to legislate and to amend is limited and judicially

Doctrines - I: Severability, Eclipse, Colourable Legislation
1. Doctrine of Severability (Separability) - under Art 13, when only a part of a law offends the Constitution, the court
strikes down only that offending part if it can be separated from the rest;
2. If the valid and invalid parts are inseparable, the whole law falls (A.K. Gopalan, 1950, where only s.14 of the Preventive
Detention Act was voided; R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla, 1957).
3. Doctrine of Eclipse - a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is not dead but dormant;
4. The dormant law stays valid for past transactions and for people who cannot claim that right (for example, those who
are not citizens, for Art 19 rights).
When an amendment removes the conflict, it revives automatically (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P., 1955).
5. It does not apply the same way to post-Constitution laws violating Fundamental Rights, which are void from inception
(Deep Chand, 1959;
6. Mahendra Lal Jaini, 1963), though such a law may still operate against non-citizens where the right is available only to
citizens.
7. Doctrine of Colourable Legislation - 'what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly'.
8. a legislature cannot use a subject within its competence as a mere pretence to legislate on a subject outside it.
9. The test goes to legislative competence, not to the motive or bona fides of the legislature (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v.
State of Orissa, 1953).
Doctrines - II: Pith and Substance, Harmonious Construction, Territorial Nexus, Repugnancy
1. Pith and Substance - to test a law against the Seventh Schedule the court looks at its true nature and character, not its
form;
2. If in pith and substance it falls within the legislature's own List, an incidental encroachment on another List does not
invalidate it (Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee, 1947, Privy Council; F.N. Balsara, 1951).
3. Harmonious Construction - overlapping provisions or List entries must be read so as to give effect to both, and one
should not be so construed as to render the other nugatory;
4. It is used to reconcile Fundamental Rights with DPSPs (In re Kerala Education Bill, 1957; Minerva Mills, 1980).
5. Doctrine of Territorial Nexus: under Art 245(1), a State law normally applies only within that State.
A State law that operates outside the State is still valid if there is a real (not illusory) connection between the State and
the object taxed or regulated (State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala, 1957);
6. Art 245(2) protects Parliament's laws absolutely - no law of Parliament is invalid merely because it operates
extra-territorially.
7. Doctrine of Repugnancy - Art 254(1): on a Concurrent List subject, if a State law is repugnant to a Parliamentary law or
an existing law, the Union law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy;
8. Art 254(2): but if the State law was reserved for and received the President's assent, it prevails in that State - subject
to Parliament's power to later add to, amend or repeal it.

- Not Mentioned - Federation, Judicial Review, Vice President removal, Offices of leader of house and leader of opposition
- Mentioned but not defined - Minority, Martial law, Untouchability, Cabinet - Added by 44th CAA but without defining

## Chapter 4
Amendments And Basic Structure

### PYQs

- **[2025]** Indian Constitution has conferred the amending power on the ordinary legislative institutions with a
few procedural hurdles. In view of this statement, examine the procedural and substantive limitations on
the amending power of the Parliament to change the Constitution. (15)

- **[2019]** "Parliament's power to amend the Constitution is a limited power and it cannot be enlarged into
absolute power." In the light of this statement explain whether Parliament under Article 368 of the
Constitution can destroy the Basic Structure of the Constitution by expanding its amending power? (15)
Under Article 368, the Parliament is granted the power to amend the Constitution by way of addition,
variation, or repeal of any provision.
Amendment Procedure in
Detail
1. Initiation: A bill for
amendment can be introduced
in either House of Parliament
(Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha),
never in state legislatures.
2. It can be introduced by a
Minister or a Private Member
and does not require prior
presidential permission.
3. Special Majority: The bill must
be passed in each House by a
Special Majority:
a. A majority (more than 50%)
of the total membership of
that House.
b. A majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting.
4. Each House must pass the bill separately. There is no provision for a joint sitting in case of a deadlock
over a constitutional amendment.
5. State Ratification: If the amendment seeks to change federal provisions (Eg. election of the President,
powers of the SC/HCs, or Seventh Schedule), it must also be ratified by the legislatures of at least half of
the states by a simple majority.
6. Presidential Assent: The President must give assent; they can neither withhold it nor return the bill for
reconsideration (as per the 24th Amendment, 1971).
Significance of Amendment
1. Ensures the Constitution remains a "living document" that adapts to evolving socio-political and
economic realities. Eg. 101st Amendment to modernize India's complex tax structure.

### [Smash Mains Source Page 32](pages/mains/mains_page_032.pdf)

2. Social Engineering: Eg. The 103rd Amendment provided 10% reservation for the Economically Weaker
Sections (EWS).
3. Correction of Anomalies: Allows the state to correct judicial interpretations that may hinder urgent
national policy goals. Eg. 1st Amendment created the Ninth Schedule to protect land reform laws from
judicial review.
4. Federal Balancing: Provides a mechanism to re-negotiate the power-sharing balance between the
Centre and the States.
5. Rights Evolution: Eg. The 86th Amendment made the "Right to Education" a Fundamental Right under
Article 21A.
6. Institutional Reform: Eg. The 121st Amendment (though struck down) attempted to create the National
Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC).
Limitations of Amendment powers of Parliament
Procedural Limitations
These are explicit constitutional conditions laid down in Article 368.
1. Special Majority Requirement - Majority of total membership of each House, and Two-thirds of
members present and voting.
2. Separate Approval by Each House - No joint sitting is allowed under Article 108.
3. Ratification by Half States for Federal Provisions - Eg. 101st Amendment (GST) required ratification.
4. Presidential Assent under Article 368(2).
5. Bill must follow all legislative procedures - notice, debate, quorum, and voting. Procedural irregularities
can invite judicial scrutiny (as per Raj Narain v. Indira Gandhi, 1975).
Substantive Limitations on the Amending Power
Judicially evolved constraints that restrict Parliament from altering core identity of Constitution
1. Doctrine of Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973))
2. Limited Amending Power Itself is Basic Structure (Minerva Mills, 1980) - Clauses (4) and (5) of Article
368 (inserted by the 42nd Amendment) were struck down.
3. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) held that even laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 1973 are
open to Basic Structure review.
4. Parliament cannot amend to abrogate or emasculate Fundamental Rights forming part of the Basic
Structure (Eg. equality, liberty).
5. Parliament cannot alter the essential federal balance between Centre and States. (Kuldip Nayar v. Union
of India (2006))
Other criticisms
1. Frequent Changes: With over 106 amendments in 75 years, critics argue the Constitution is amended too
easily compared to the US.
2. Central Dominance: State legislatures cannot initiate amendments, leaving them dependent on the
Centre's political will.
3. Ambiguity of "Basic Structure": Since the SC hasn't exhaustively defined "Basic Structure," it leads to
uncertainty and potential judicial overreach.
4. No Joint Sitting: A small minority in the Rajya Sabha can block a critical amendment favored by a
massive Lok Sabha majority.

Major SC Judgments related to Amendment
1. Shankari Prasad Case (1951): Ruled that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including
Fundamental Rights.
2. Golaknath Case (1967): Reversed the previous stance, ruling that Fundamental Rights are
"transcendental" and cannot be amended.
3. Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973): Created the Basic Structure Doctrine, limiting the Parliament's
power.
4. Minerva Mills Case (1980): Reaffirmed that the Parliament's power to amend is limited and cannot be
used to grant itself unlimited power.
Major Amendments in Article 368
1. 24th Amendment (1971): Clarified that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution and made it
obligatory for the President to give assent.
2. 42nd Amendment (1976): Attempted to declare that there shall be no limitation whatsoever on the
constituent power of Parliament; this was later invalidated by the SC in Minerva Mills.

1. Proper synthesis between the British principle of Parliamentary sovereignty(Parliament has the sole authority over law

2. American principle of judicial supremacy(judiciary the ultimate authority to interpret the Constitution and laws of a

1. SC at top of hierarchy then HC for one or more states below SC then below it subordinate courts.

Fundamental Rights
1. Six Fundamental Rights, in Part III (Arts 12 to 35).

DPSPs
1. Contained in Part IV (Arts 36 to 51).
2. Promote the ideal of social and economic democracy.

1. Ten Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh
Committee.
2. The eleventh, on providing education to a child between six and fourteen, was added by the 86th Amendment, 2002, so
there are eleven in all.

4. Not directly enforceable by any court, but given effect through ordinary statutes.
Secular State
Indian secularism means the State has no religion of its own and gives equal respect to all faiths, rather than the Western
wall of separation between religion and State.
It ensures
1. that one religious community does not dominate another;
2. that some members do not dominate other members of the same religious community;
3. that the State neither enforces any particular religion nor takes away the religious freedom of individuals.

PREAMBLE
Introduction [PRELIMS 2021,2017]
1. Origin: The US Constitution was the first to begin with a Preamble.
2. Philosophy: Contains the philosophy and basic values of the Constitution; called its “identity card” (N.A. Palkhivala),
“soul” (Thakurdas Bhargava) and “horoscope” (K.M. Munshi).
3. Source: Based on Nehru’s Objectives Resolution, moved on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947.
4. Amendment: “Socialist,” “Secular” and “Integrity” added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, the only amendment so
far; their insertion was upheld by the SC in Balram Singh v Union of India (2024).
5. Source of authority: Declares the people of India as the source of authority of the Constitution; the Preamble itself
is neither a source of power to the legislature nor a limit on it.
6. Non-justiciable: Not enforceable in courts on its own; its ideals work through other provisions.
7. Interpretation: States the ideals and objectives, and helps interpret provisions where the text is ambiguous.
8. Aspirations: Reflects the aspirations of the people to be achieved.
Preamble: Keywords and Objectives [PRELIMS 2017]
Order of words: “Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic”. The original Preamble (adopted 26 November 1949)
read “Sovereign Democratic Republic”; Socialist, Secular and Integrity were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
1. Sovereign
- India is neither a dependency nor a dominion; internally supreme and externally free from foreign control.
Commonwealth or UN membership does not dilute it.
- Can acquire foreign territory; but ceding Indian territory needs a constitutional amendment (Art 368), not an
ordinary law under Art 3 (In re Berubari Union, 1960, advisory opinion). Eg. 9th Amendment, 1960 (Berubari); 100th
Amendment, 2015 (Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh).
2. Socialist (42nd Amendment, 1976)
- Democratic socialism: a mixed economy where public and private sectors coexist; not communistic socialism or
state ownership of everything. Aims at a welfare State through DPSPs, without abolishing private property.
- Dr Balram Singh v Union of India (25 November 2024): SC upheld the insertion of “socialist” and “secular”;
“socialist” means a welfare State and does not restrict economic policy.
3. Secular (42nd Amendment, 1976)
- The idea already existed in Arts 14 to 16 and 25 to 28.
- No State religion; the State neither favours nor penalises any faith.
- Positive secularism: equal respect for all religions (sarva dharma sambhava), not the Western “wall of separation”.
- Part of the Basic Structure (S.R. Bommai, 1994).
4. Democratic
- Popular sovereignty: “We, the People of India” are the source of authority.
- Indirect (representative) parliamentary democracy, not direct democracy; referendum, initiative and recall are not
part of the constitutional scheme.
- Pillars:
- Universal adult franchise (Art 326; voting age lowered from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment, 1988)
- Periodic free and fair elections
- One person, one vote
- An independent judiciary and rule of law
- Aims at political, social and economic democracy, echoing Ambedkar’s warning about a “life of contradictions”.
5. Republic
- Head of State is elected, not hereditary: the President is indirectly elected for a fixed 5 year term (Arts 52, 54, 55),
unlike the British Crown.
- Political sovereignty rests with the people; no privileged class; all public offices open to every citizen without
discrimination.

### [Prelims Source Page 21](pages/prelims/prelims_page_021.pdf)

Objectives: Justice is taken from the Russian Revolution (1917); Liberty, Equality and Fraternity from the French Revolution
(1789).
6. Justice: Social, Economic, Political
- Social justice: no discrimination on grounds of caste, religion, sex etc. (Arts 15, 16, 17, 46).
- Economic justice: removal of gross inequalities in wealth and income (Arts 38, 39).
- Political justice: equal political rights and equal access to public office.
- Secured through a mix of Fundamental Rights and DPSPs.
7. Liberty: of Thought, Expression, Belief, Faith and Worship
- The Preamble secures only these five liberties; not “action” or “conscience”.
- Means absence of arbitrary restraint plus conditions for full development of personality.
- Not absolute: Art 19 rights are subject to reasonable restrictions.
8. Equality: of Status and Opportunity
- Core idea: absence of special privileges.
- Civic: Arts 14 to 18. Political: Arts 325, 326. Economic: Art 39(d) (equal pay for equal work).
9. Fraternity
- A sense of common brotherhood, promoted through single citizenship.
- Assures both (i) dignity of the individual and (ii) unity and integrity of the Nation; “Integrity” added in 1976.
- Reinforced by Fundamental Duty Art 51A(e).
Traps
- Word order: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.
- Justice from the Russian Revolution; Liberty, Equality, Fraternity from the French Revolution.
- Fraternity covers both dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the Nation.
- Liberty lists five items only; action and conscience are not among them.
Is the Preamble amendable? The 42nd Amendment, 1976
1. Can it be amended? Yes. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held the Preamble is part of the Constitution, so it can be
amended under Art 368, but not in a way that destroys its basic features.
2. Amended only once, by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, which:
- added “Socialist” and “Secular”, and
- changed “unity of the Nation” to “unity and integrity of the Nation”.
- So on 26 January 1950, India was a “Sovereign Democratic Republic”.
3. Not a source of power for the legislature, nor a limit on its powers.
4. Non-justiciable, but a “key to open the mind of the makers” (Berubari, 1960); used to resolve ambiguity in the text.
5. LIC v Consumer Education and Research Centre (1995) reaffirmed it as an integral part of the Constitution.
6. Insertion of “socialist” and “secular” upheld in Dr Balram Singh v Union of India (2024)

BASIC STRUCTURE DOCTRINE
Basic Structure Doctrine - Evolution
1. The question - How far does Art 368 lets Parliament amend the Constitution.
2. Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965): Parliament can amend even Fundamental Rights, because a
Constitutional Amendment is not a 'law' under Art 13.
3. Golak Nath (1967): reversed this - Fundamental Rights are transcendental and cannot be abridged by amendment.
4. Parliament replied with the 24th Amendment, 1971, inserting Art 13(4) & Art 368(3) to put amendments outside Art 13.
5. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) - a 13-judge bench, the largest ever, by 7:6 overruled Golak Nath and laid
down the middle path: Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot
alter, damage or destroy its 'Basic Structure'.
6. The 42nd Amendment, 1976 then added two clauses:
(a) Art 368(4): no amendment can be questioned in any court;
(b) Art 368(5): Parliament's amending power has no limit.
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down both, holding that limited amending power is itself a basic feature.
7. Waman Rao (1981) fixed 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda) as the cut-off from which the doctrine applies.
8. Note that the Constitution nowhere defines the Basic Structure - it is entirely judge-made, and the list is illustrative, not
exhaustive.
Basic Structure - What is a held to be a part of it
1. Supremacy of the Constitution;
2. Rule of law; the sovereign, democratic and republican character of the polity;
3. Secular character (S.R. Bommai, 1994); federal character and the unity and integrity of the nation;
4. Separation of powers between the 3 organs;
5. Judicial review and the powers of the Supreme Court under Arts 32, 136, 141, 142 and of High Courts under Arts 226,
227 (I.R. Coelho, 2007). independence of the judiciary;
6. Free and fair elections (Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975, which struck down Art 329A);
7. The Parliamentary System;
8. Harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs and the Limited Amending Power of Parliament
(Minerva Mills, 1980);
9. Effective access to justice;
10. Welfare State goals;
11. Art 21 - the rule of law and life and liberty.

AMENDING PROCEDURE
1. Special Majority: Art 368(2) [PRELIMS 2024, 2022]
CONDITION
- Any amendment not covered by the proviso to Art 368(2), i.e. one that does not affect the federal provisions or the
Seventh Schedule.
- Examples: Fundamental Rights, DPSPs, and most other provisions.
MAJORITY NEEDED
- Special majority in each House: a majority of the total membership and 2/3 of members present and voting.
- Presidential assent is mandatory (24th CAA, 1971).
- The Basic Structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) limits this amending power.
2. Special Majority + State Ratification: Proviso to Art 368(2) [PRELIMS 2013]
CONDITION: the amendment affects any of the following:
1. Election of the President (Arts 54, 55);
2. Extent of the executive power of the Union and the States (Arts 73, 162);
3. The Supreme Court, the High Courts, and High Courts for UTs (Art 241);
4. Distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States, and any List in the Seventh Schedule;
5. GST Council (Art 279A, added by the 101st CAA, 2016);
6. Representation of States in Parliament;
7. Article 368 itself.
MAJORITY NEEDED
- Special majority in each House, plus ratification by the legislatures of not less than half the States, by simple
majority.

## Chapter 4
Amendments And Basic Structure

### PYQs

- **[2025]** Indian Constitution has conferred the amending power on the ordinary legislative institutions with a
few procedural hurdles. In view of this statement, examine the procedural and substantive limitations on
the amending power of the Parliament to change the Constitution. (15)

- **[2019]** "Parliament's power to amend the Constitution is a limited power and it cannot be enlarged into
absolute power." In the light of this statement explain whether Parliament under Article 368 of the
Constitution can destroy the Basic Structure of the Constitution by expanding its amending power? (15)
Under Article 368, the Parliament is granted the power to amend the Constitution by way of addition,
variation, or repeal of any provision.
Amendment Procedure in
Detail
1. Initiation: A bill for
amendment can be introduced
in either House of Parliament
(Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha),
never in state legislatures.
2. It can be introduced by a
Minister or a Private Member
and does not require prior
presidential permission.
3. Special Majority: The bill must
be passed in each House by a
Special Majority:
a. A majority (more than 50%)
of the total membership of
that House.
b. A majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting.
4. Each House must pass the bill separately. There is no provision for a joint sitting in case of a deadlock
over a constitutional amendment.
5. State Ratification: If the amendment seeks to change federal provisions (Eg. election of the President,
powers of the SC/HCs, or Seventh Schedule), it must also be ratified by the legislatures of at least half of
the states by a simple majority.
6. Presidential Assent: The President must give assent; they can neither withhold it nor return the bill for
reconsideration (as per the 24th Amendment, 1971).
Significance of Amendment
1. Ensures the Constitution remains a "living document" that adapts to evolving socio-political and
economic realities. Eg. 101st Amendment to modernize India's complex tax structure.

2. Social Engineering: Eg. The 103rd Amendment provided 10% reservation for the Economically Weaker
Sections (EWS).
3. Correction of Anomalies: Allows the state to correct judicial interpretations that may hinder urgent
national policy goals. Eg. 1st Amendment created the Ninth Schedule to protect land reform laws from
judicial review.
4. Federal Balancing: Provides a mechanism to re-negotiate the power-sharing balance between the
Centre and the States.
5. Rights Evolution: Eg. The 86th Amendment made the "Right to Education" a Fundamental Right under
Article 21A.
6. Institutional Reform: Eg. The 121st Amendment (though struck down) attempted to create the National
Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC).
Limitations of Amendment powers of Parliament
Procedural Limitations
These are explicit constitutional conditions laid down in Article 368.
1. Special Majority Requirement - Majority of total membership of each House, and Two-thirds of
members present and voting.
2. Separate Approval by Each House - No joint sitting is allowed under Article 108.
3. Ratification by Half States for Federal Provisions - Eg. 101st Amendment (GST) required ratification.
4. Presidential Assent under Article 368(2).
5. Bill must follow all legislative procedures - notice, debate, quorum, and voting. Procedural irregularities
can invite judicial scrutiny (as per Raj Narain v. Indira Gandhi, 1975).
Substantive Limitations on the Amending Power
Judicially evolved constraints that restrict Parliament from altering core identity of Constitution
1. Doctrine of Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973))
2. Limited Amending Power Itself is Basic Structure (Minerva Mills, 1980) - Clauses (4) and (5) of Article
368 (inserted by the 42nd Amendment) were struck down.
3. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) held that even laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 1973 are
open to Basic Structure review.
4. Parliament cannot amend to abrogate or emasculate Fundamental Rights forming part of the Basic
Structure (Eg. equality, liberty).
5. Parliament cannot alter the essential federal balance between Centre and States. (Kuldip Nayar v. Union
of India (2006))
Other criticisms
1. Frequent Changes: With over 106 amendments in 75 years, critics argue the Constitution is amended too
easily compared to the US.
2. Central Dominance: State legislatures cannot initiate amendments, leaving them dependent on the
Centre's political will.
3. Ambiguity of "Basic Structure": Since the SC hasn't exhaustively defined "Basic Structure," it leads to
uncertainty and potential judicial overreach.
4. No Joint Sitting: A small minority in the Rajya Sabha can block a critical amendment favored by a
massive Lok Sabha majority.

Major SC Judgments related to Amendment
1. Shankari Prasad Case (1951): Ruled that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including
Fundamental Rights.
2. Golaknath Case (1967): Reversed the previous stance, ruling that Fundamental Rights are
"transcendental" and cannot be amended.
3. Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973): Created the Basic Structure Doctrine, limiting the Parliament's
power.
4. Minerva Mills Case (1980): Reaffirmed that the Parliament's power to amend is limited and cannot be
used to grant itself unlimited power.
Major Amendments in Article 368
1. 24th Amendment (1971): Clarified that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution and made it
obligatory for the President to give assent.
2. 42nd Amendment (1976): Attempted to declare that there shall be no limitation whatsoever on the
constituent power of Parliament; this was later invalidated by the SC in Minerva Mills.

Constitution and Constitutional Government [PRELIMS 2023,2021,2020,2014]
1. A Constitution is the fundamental law that constitutes the organs of government and allocates power among them, but
its chief purpose is to define and limit the powers of government.
2. Constitutional government therefore means limited government - a government bound by the terms of the
Constitution.
3. It places effective restrictions on the authority of the State in the interest of individual liberty, not restrictions on liberty
in the interest of State authority.
4. The devices of limitation in India:
(a) Justiciable Fundamental Rights (Part III), enforceable under Arts 32 and 226.
(b) Judicial review.
(c) Federal division of powers under the Seventh Schedule.
(d) An independent judiciary.
(e) The Basic Structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).
5. A government may be popular, elected or multi-party and still not be constitutional if it is not legally limited.

Due Process of Law vs Procedure Established by Law [PRELIMS 2023]
1. Article 21 as drafted adopted the 'procedure established by law' formula (traced to the Japanese Constitution): the
court asks only whether a competent legislature validly enacted the law and whether its procedure was followed.
2. 'Due process of law' (US 5th and 14th Amendments) goes further and requires the law and its procedure to be fair, just
and reasonable - in essence it embodies the principles of natural justice (nemo judex in causa sua - no one a judge in his
own cause; audi alteram partem - hear the other side).
3. In A.K. Gopalan v State of Madras (1950) the Supreme Court read Art 21 literally;
4. In Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978) it held that the procedure under Art 21 must be 'right, just and fair and not
arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive', effectively reading due process into the Constitution.
State, Government, Democracy and Bureaucracy [PRELIMS 2021,2020,2017]
1. In political theory the State has four essential elements - population, a definite territory, a government, and
sovereignty (independence of external control). Hence the correct definition is a community of persons permanently
occupying a definite territory, independent of external control and possessing an organised government;
2. long residence, common culture or tradition make a nation or a society, not a State.
3. The State is permanent and wider;
4. The government is only its agency and changes.
5. (Note: Art 12 gives a separate and wider working definition of 'the State' for the purposes of Part III.) Democracy's
superior virtue is that it calls into activity the intelligence and character of ordinary men and women, resting on
participation, accountability and universal adult franchise rather than on a single dynamic leader.
6. The bureaucracy is the permanent, politically neutral civil service whose characteristic function is the implementation of
public policy framed by the political executive;
7. Art 311 safeguards and the All India Services underpin it.
Rule of Law and Separation of Powers [PRELIMS 2021,2018]
1. Rule of Law comes from Britain and was explained by A.V. Dicey. It has three parts:
(a) Supremacy of law: no arbitrary power; the powers of government are limited.
(b) Equality before law: embodied in Art 14.
(c) Predominance of legal spirit: ordinary courts protect liberty and civil rights.
2. It does not include any 'responsibility of the people to the government';
3. The direction of accountability runs the other way.
4. The Rule of Law is part of the Basic Structure (Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain, 1975).
5. Separation of powers - the organic and functional distribution of authority among the legislature, executive and judiciary
with checks and balances - is regarded as the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy because it prevents
concentration of power;
6. India follows it functionally rather than absolutely (Art 50 separates the judiciary from the executive), and it too is part of
the Basic Structure.
Citizenship (Part II, Articles 5-11) [PRELIMS 2021]
1. India has single citizenship and a single domicile - there is no separate State citizenship, unlike the USA.
2. Arts 5-11 (Part II) deal only with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution;
3. Art 11 empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship by law, under which the Citizenship Act, 1955 was enacted.
4. It provides five modes of acquisition - birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory - and
three modes of loss - renunciation, termination and deprivation.
5. The Central Government can deprive a registered or naturalised citizen of citizenship if the person:
(a) obtained it by fraud;
(b) showed disloyalty to the Constitution;
(c) traded or communicated with the enemy during a war;
(d) was sentenced to two years' imprisonment within five years of registration or naturalisation;
(e) lived outside India for seven years continuously.
So citizenship, once granted, is not indefeasible.

Liberty, Equality, Rights and Social Capital [PRELIMS 2019,2018,2017]
1. Liberty is not mere absence of restraint or the opportunity to do whatever one likes;
2. in its positive sense it is the opportunity to develop oneself fully.
3. Law and liberty are complementary, not opposed - 'where there is no law there is no liberty' (John Locke) - because law
restrains interference by others and creates the conditions of freedom;
4. more laws do not automatically mean less liberty.
5. Equality implies primarily the absence of special privileges and equality of opportunity;
6. It does not mean absence of restraint, competition or ideology.
7. Rights are claims of the citizen against the State, recognised and enforced by it - not claims of the State against citizens
nor privileges of a few;
8. in India they are made justiciable through Part III read with Arts 32 and 226.
9. Social capital is a distinct, intangible resource - the level of mutual trust, harmony, networks and reciprocity in a society
- as opposed to physical capital (buildings, infrastructure, machines) and human capital (literacy, skills, working-age
population).
Constitutionalism and Constitutional Morality
1. Constitutionalism is the doctrine that governmental power must be limited by and exercised through law - 'limited
government'.
2. A country may possess a Constitution without having constitutionalism (authoritarian regimes have written
constitutions but unchecked power);
3. the two are therefore not the same thing.
4. Its essential ingredients are: rule of law, separation of powers with checks and balances, judicial review, enforceable
fundamental rights, an independent judiciary, free and fair periodic elections, and a government accountable to the
people.
5. Constitutional morality: a phrase Ambedkar borrowed from the historian George Grote and pressed in the Constituent
Assembly (4 November 1948).
It means following the spirit and core values of the Constitution, not mere literal legality, and the willingness of all actors
to work it with restraint.
6. Illustrations: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) - the proclamation dissolving the Bihar Assembly on the
Governor's report was held unconstitutional and mala fide;
7. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) - judicial review is part of the Basic Structure, so even Ninth Schedule laws
inserted after 24 April 1973 can be tested;
8. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) - constitutional morality prevails over popular/social morality.
Sovereignty and its Kinds
Sovereignty is the supreme, original and independent authority of the State, one of the four essential elements of a State
and the one that distinguishes a State from every other association.
KINDS OF SOVEREIGNTY
1. Internal: supremacy over all persons and associations within the territory.
2. External: freedom from foreign control in the conduct of relations with other States.
3. Legal: the authority that makes law and whose commands the courts enforce. In India the Constitution is supreme; in
Britain, Parliament.
4. Political: the electorate behind the legal sovereign, whose will ultimately prevails.
5. Popular: power flows from the people, declared in the opening words WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA and worked through
universal adult franchise.
6. De jure against de facto: legal title to rule as against actual effective control.
7. Pluralist view (Harold Laski): the State is only one association among many and not absolutely supreme.
- Parliamentary sovereignty in the United Kingdom means no court can question an Act of Parliament.
- India instead follows constitutional supremacy, so Parliament's power to legislate and to amend is limited and judicially
reviewable.

---

### [Prelims Source Page 27](pages/prelims/prelims_page_027.pdf)

Doctrines - I: Severability, Eclipse, Colourable Legislation
1. Doctrine of Severability (Separability) - under Art 13, when only a part of a law offends the Constitution, the court
strikes down only that offending part if it can be separated from the rest;
2. If the valid and invalid parts are inseparable, the whole law falls (A.K. Gopalan, 1950, where only s.14 of the Preventive
Detention Act was voided; R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla, 1957).
3. Doctrine of Eclipse - a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is not dead but dormant;
4. The dormant law stays valid for past transactions and for people who cannot claim that right (for example, those who
are not citizens, for Art 19 rights).
When an amendment removes the conflict, it revives automatically (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P., 1955).
5. It does not apply the same way to post-Constitution laws violating Fundamental Rights, which are void from inception
(Deep Chand, 1959;
6. Mahendra Lal Jaini, 1963), though such a law may still operate against non-citizens where the right is available only to
citizens.
7. Doctrine of Colourable Legislation - 'what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly'.
8. a legislature cannot use a subject within its competence as a mere pretence to legislate on a subject outside it.
9. The test goes to legislative competence, not to the motive or bona fides of the legislature (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v.
State of Orissa, 1953).
Doctrines - II: Pith and Substance, Harmonious Construction, Territorial Nexus, Repugnancy
1. Pith and Substance - to test a law against the Seventh Schedule the court looks at its true nature and character, not its
form;
2. If in pith and substance it falls within the legislature's own List, an incidental encroachment on another List does not
invalidate it (Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee, 1947, Privy Council; F.N. Balsara, 1951).
3. Harmonious Construction - overlapping provisions or List entries must be read so as to give effect to both, and one
should not be so construed as to render the other nugatory;
4. It is used to reconcile Fundamental Rights with DPSPs (In re Kerala Education Bill, 1957; Minerva Mills, 1980).
5. Doctrine of Territorial Nexus: under Art 245(1), a State law normally applies only within that State.
A State law that operates outside the State is still valid if there is a real (not illusory) connection between the State and
the object taxed or regulated (State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala, 1957);
6. Art 245(2) protects Parliament's laws absolutely - no law of Parliament is invalid merely because it operates
extra-territorially.
7. Doctrine of Repugnancy - Art 254(1): on a Concurrent List subject, if a State law is repugnant to a Parliamentary law or
an existing law, the Union law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy;
8. Art 254(2): but if the State law was reserved for and received the President's assent, it prevails in that State - subject
to Parliament's power to later add to, amend or repeal it.
TERMS WHERE THE CONSTITUTION IS NOT CLEAR
- Not Mentioned - Federation, Judicial Review, Vice President removal, Offices of leader of house and leader of opposition
- Mentioned but not defined - Minority, Martial law, Untouchability, Cabinet - Added by 44th CAA but without defining

## Chapter 4
Amendments And Basic Structure

### PYQs

- **[2025]** Indian Constitution has conferred the amending power on the ordinary legislative institutions with a
few procedural hurdles. In view of this statement, examine the procedural and substantive limitations on
the amending power of the Parliament to change the Constitution. (15)

- **[2019]** "Parliament's power to amend the Constitution is a limited power and it cannot be enlarged into
absolute power." In the light of this statement explain whether Parliament under Article 368 of the
Constitution can destroy the Basic Structure of the Constitution by expanding its amending power? (15)
Under Article 368, the Parliament is granted the power to amend the Constitution by way of addition,
variation, or repeal of any provision.
Amendment Procedure in
Detail
1. Initiation: A bill for
amendment can be introduced
in either House of Parliament
(Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha),
never in state legislatures.
2. It can be introduced by a
Minister or a Private Member
and does not require prior
presidential permission.
3. Special Majority: The bill must
be passed in each House by a
Special Majority:
a. A majority (more than 50%)
of the total membership of
that House.
b. A majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting.
4. Each House must pass the bill separately. There is no provision for a joint sitting in case of a deadlock
over a constitutional amendment.
5. State Ratification: If the amendment seeks to change federal provisions (Eg. election of the President,
powers of the SC/HCs, or Seventh Schedule), it must also be ratified by the legislatures of at least half of
the states by a simple majority.
6. Presidential Assent: The President must give assent; they can neither withhold it nor return the bill for
reconsideration (as per the 24th Amendment, 1971).
Significance of Amendment
1. Ensures the Constitution remains a "living document" that adapts to evolving socio-political and
economic realities. Eg. 101st Amendment to modernize India's complex tax structure.

2. Social Engineering: Eg. The 103rd Amendment provided 10% reservation for the Economically Weaker
Sections (EWS).
3. Correction of Anomalies: Allows the state to correct judicial interpretations that may hinder urgent
national policy goals. Eg. 1st Amendment created the Ninth Schedule to protect land reform laws from
judicial review.
4. Federal Balancing: Provides a mechanism to re-negotiate the power-sharing balance between the
Centre and the States.
5. Rights Evolution: Eg. The 86th Amendment made the "Right to Education" a Fundamental Right under
Article 21A.
6. Institutional Reform: Eg. The 121st Amendment (though struck down) attempted to create the National
Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC).
Limitations of Amendment powers of Parliament
Procedural Limitations
These are explicit constitutional conditions laid down in Article 368.
1. Special Majority Requirement - Majority of total membership of each House, and Two-thirds of
members present and voting.
2. Separate Approval by Each House - No joint sitting is allowed under Article 108.
3. Ratification by Half States for Federal Provisions - Eg. 101st Amendment (GST) required ratification.
4. Presidential Assent under Article 368(2).
5. Bill must follow all legislative procedures - notice, debate, quorum, and voting. Procedural irregularities
can invite judicial scrutiny (as per Raj Narain v. Indira Gandhi, 1975).
Substantive Limitations on the Amending Power
Judicially evolved constraints that restrict Parliament from altering core identity of Constitution
1. Doctrine of Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973))
2. Limited Amending Power Itself is Basic Structure (Minerva Mills, 1980) - Clauses (4) and (5) of Article
368 (inserted by the 42nd Amendment) were struck down.
3. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) held that even laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 1973 are
open to Basic Structure review.
4. Parliament cannot amend to abrogate or emasculate Fundamental Rights forming part of the Basic
Structure (Eg. equality, liberty).
5. Parliament cannot alter the essential federal balance between Centre and States. (Kuldip Nayar v. Union
of India (2006))
Other criticisms
1. Frequent Changes: With over 106 amendments in 75 years, critics argue the Constitution is amended too
easily compared to the US.
2. Central Dominance: State legislatures cannot initiate amendments, leaving them dependent on the
Centre's political will.
3. Ambiguity of "Basic Structure": Since the SC hasn't exhaustively defined "Basic Structure," it leads to
uncertainty and potential judicial overreach.
4. No Joint Sitting: A small minority in the Rajya Sabha can block a critical amendment favored by a
massive Lok Sabha majority.

Major SC Judgments related to Amendment
1. Shankari Prasad Case (1951): Ruled that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including
Fundamental Rights.
2. Golaknath Case (1967): Reversed the previous stance, ruling that Fundamental Rights are
"transcendental" and cannot be amended.
3. Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973): Created the Basic Structure Doctrine, limiting the Parliament's
power.
4. Minerva Mills Case (1980): Reaffirmed that the Parliament's power to amend is limited and cannot be
used to grant itself unlimited power.
Major Amendments in Article 368
1. 24th Amendment (1971): Clarified that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution and made it
obligatory for the President to give assent.
2. 42nd Amendment (1976): Attempted to declare that there shall be no limitation whatsoever on the
constituent power of Parliament; this was later invalidated by the SC in Minerva Mills.

PREAMBLE, NATURE, PARTS & SCHEDULES

### THEME ANALYSIS
1. REPEATS

#### A. Preamble and its Keywords
- On 26 January 1950 India was a Sovereign Democratic Republic; Socialist and Secular came in 1976 [2021].
- Economic liberty is no Preamble objective; the Preamble mirrors the makers' mind [2017].
- It is part of the Constitution but has no independent legal effect [2020].

#### B. Parts, Schedules and Concluding Articles
- Part IXA municipalities, Part XVIII emergency, Part XX amendment [2024].
- Seventh Schedule traps: inter State quarantine is Union [2024]; education spans many provisions [2012].
- Eighth Schedule holds 22 languages [2024, 2008]; classical language status is separate [2015, 2014].

#### C. Ninth and Tenth Schedules
- The Ninth Schedule came with the First Amendment, 1951; entries after 1973 face Basic Structure review [2019,
2018].
- The Tenth Schedule carries anti defection [2014]; the presiding officer decides with no time frame [2022].
- Political party appears in the Constitution only through the Tenth Schedule [2025].

#### D. Basic Features and Core Concepts
- A Constitution defines and limits government power [2023, 2021, 2020, 2014].
- Rule of law: limitation of powers, equality before law, liberty and civil rights [2018].
- Separation of powers best safeguards liberty [2021]; due process means natural justice [2023].
- Concept staples: liberty [2019, 2018], rights against the State, equality as absence of privileges [2017].
2. HOW THE FORMAT HAS CHANGED
- 2008 to 2014: direct recall of Schedules, languages and anti defection [2008, 2012, 2014]
- 2017 to 2023: one best answer concept questions on liberty, rule of law, State and constitutional government [2017,
2019, 2021, 2023]
- 2024 to 2025: multi statement sets on Parts, Lists and ratification [2024, 2025]
- 2026: the "which conclusion is correct" format, judging three statements together [2026]
3. WHAT IS BEING ASKED NOW
- The bare text: which Part holds what [2024], subjects needing State ratification [2025], Articles that name the
Constitution, repeal the old Acts and fix commencement [2026]
- Tenth Schedule detail: who decides disqualification, and whether "political party" is mentioned [2025]
- One concept question per paper still appears [2023]

PREAMBLE
Introduction [PRELIMS 2021,2017]
1. Origin: The US Constitution was the first to begin with a Preamble.
2. Philosophy: Contains the philosophy and basic values of the Constitution; called its “identity card” (N.A. Palkhivala),
“soul” (Thakurdas Bhargava) and “horoscope” (K.M. Munshi).
3. Source: Based on Nehru’s Objectives Resolution, moved on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947.
4. Amendment: “Socialist,” “Secular” and “Integrity” added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, the only amendment so
far; their insertion was upheld by the SC in Balram Singh v Union of India (2024).
5. Source of authority: Declares the people of India as the source of authority of the Constitution; the Preamble itself
is neither a source of power to the legislature nor a limit on it.
6. Non-justiciable: Not enforceable in courts on its own; its ideals work through other provisions.
7. Interpretation: States the ideals and objectives, and helps interpret provisions where the text is ambiguous.
8. Aspirations: Reflects the aspirations of the people to be achieved.
Preamble: Keywords and Objectives [PRELIMS 2017]
Order of words: “Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic”. The original Preamble (adopted 26 November 1949)
read “Sovereign Democratic Republic”; Socialist, Secular and Integrity were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
1. Sovereign
- India is neither a dependency nor a dominion; internally supreme and externally free from foreign control.
Commonwealth or UN membership does not dilute it.
- Can acquire foreign territory; but ceding Indian territory needs a constitutional amendment (Art 368), not an
ordinary law under Art 3 (In re Berubari Union, 1960, advisory opinion). Eg. 9th Amendment, 1960 (Berubari); 100th
Amendment, 2015 (Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh).
2. Socialist (42nd Amendment, 1976)
- Democratic socialism: a mixed economy where public and private sectors coexist; not communistic socialism or
state ownership of everything. Aims at a welfare State through DPSPs, without abolishing private property.
- Dr Balram Singh v Union of India (25 November 2024): SC upheld the insertion of “socialist” and “secular”;
“socialist” means a welfare State and does not restrict economic policy.
3. Secular (42nd Amendment, 1976)
- The idea already existed in Arts 14 to 16 and 25 to 28.
- No State religion; the State neither favours nor penalises any faith.
- Positive secularism: equal respect for all religions (sarva dharma sambhava), not the Western “wall of separation”.
- Part of the Basic Structure (S.R. Bommai, 1994).
4. Democratic
- Popular sovereignty: “We, the People of India” are the source of authority.
- Indirect (representative) parliamentary democracy, not direct democracy; referendum, initiative and recall are not
part of the constitutional scheme.
- Pillars:
- Universal adult franchise (Art 326; voting age lowered from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment, 1988)
- Periodic free and fair elections
- One person, one vote
- An independent judiciary and rule of law
- Aims at political, social and economic democracy, echoing Ambedkar’s warning about a “life of contradictions”.
5. Republic
- Head of State is elected, not hereditary: the President is indirectly elected for a fixed 5 year term (Arts 52, 54, 55),
unlike the British Crown.
- Political sovereignty rests with the people; no privileged class; all public offices open to every citizen without
discrimination.

Constitution and Constitutional Government [PRELIMS 2023,2021,2020,2014]
1. A Constitution is the fundamental law that constitutes the organs of government and allocates power among them, but
its chief purpose is to define and limit the powers of government.
2. Constitutional government therefore means limited government - a government bound by the terms of the
Constitution.
3. It places effective restrictions on the authority of the State in the interest of individual liberty, not restrictions on liberty
in the interest of State authority.
4. The devices of limitation in India:
(a) Justiciable Fundamental Rights (Part III), enforceable under Arts 32 and 226.
(b) Judicial review.
(c) Federal division of powers under the Seventh Schedule.
(d) An independent judiciary.

Due Process of Law vs Procedure Established by Law [PRELIMS 2023]
1. Article 21 as drafted adopted the 'procedure established by law' formula (traced to the Japanese Constitution): the
court asks only whether a competent legislature validly enacted the law and whether its procedure was followed.
2. 'Due process of law' (US 5th and 14th Amendments) goes further and requires the law and its procedure to be fair, just
and reasonable - in essence it embodies the principles of natural justice (nemo judex in causa sua - no one a judge in his
own cause; audi alteram partem - hear the other side).
3. In A.K. Gopalan v State of Madras (1950) the Supreme Court read Art 21 literally;
4. In Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978) it held that the procedure under Art 21 must be 'right, just and fair and not
arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive', effectively reading due process into the Constitution.
State, Government, Democracy and Bureaucracy [PRELIMS 2021,2020,2017]
1. In political theory the State has four essential elements - population, a definite territory, a government, and
sovereignty (independence of external control). Hence the correct definition is a community of persons permanently
occupying a definite territory, independent of external control and possessing an organised government;
2. long residence, common culture or tradition make a nation or a society, not a State.
3. The State is permanent and wider;
4. The government is only its agency and changes.
5. (Note: Art 12 gives a separate and wider working definition of 'the State' for the purposes of Part III.) Democracy's
superior virtue is that it calls into activity the intelligence and character of ordinary men and women, resting on
participation, accountability and universal adult franchise rather than on a single dynamic leader.
6. The bureaucracy is the permanent, politically neutral civil service whose characteristic function is the implementation of
public policy framed by the political executive;
7. Art 311 safeguards and the All India Services underpin it.
Rule of Law and Separation of Powers [PRELIMS 2021,2018]
1. Rule of Law comes from Britain and was explained by A.V. Dicey. It has three parts:
(a) Supremacy of law: no arbitrary power; the powers of government are limited.
(b) Equality before law: embodied in Art 14.
(c) Predominance of legal spirit: ordinary courts protect liberty and civil rights.
2. It does not include any 'responsibility of the people to the government';
3. The direction of accountability runs the other way.
4. The Rule of Law is part of the Basic Structure (Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain, 1975).
5. Separation of powers - the organic and functional distribution of authority among the legislature, executive and judiciary
with checks and balances - is regarded as the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy because it prevents
concentration of power;
6. India follows it functionally rather than absolutely (Art 50 separates the judiciary from the executive), and it too is part of
the Basic Structure.
Citizenship (Part II, Articles 5-11) [PRELIMS 2021]
1. India has single citizenship and a single domicile - there is no separate State citizenship, unlike the USA.
2. Arts 5-11 (Part II) deal only with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution;
3. Art 11 empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship by law, under which the Citizenship Act, 1955 was enacted.
4. It provides five modes of acquisition - birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory - and
three modes of loss - renunciation, termination and deprivation.
5. The Central Government can deprive a registered or naturalised citizen of citizenship if the person:
(a) obtained it by fraud;
(b) showed disloyalty to the Constitution;
(c) traded or communicated with the enemy during a war;
(d) was sentenced to two years' imprisonment within five years of registration or naturalisation;
(e) lived outside India for seven years continuously.
So citizenship, once granted, is not indefeasible.

6. The President need only be a citizen of India qualified for election to the Lok Sabha (Art 58) - citizenship by birth is not
required, unlike the US requirement of a natural-born citizen.
Liberty, Equality, Rights and Social Capital [PRELIMS 2019,2018,2017]
1. Liberty is not mere absence of restraint or the opportunity to do whatever one likes;
2. in its positive sense it is the opportunity to develop oneself fully.
3. Law and liberty are complementary, not opposed - 'where there is no law there is no liberty' (John Locke) - because law
restrains interference by others and creates the conditions of freedom;
4. more laws do not automatically mean less liberty.
5. Equality implies primarily the absence of special privileges and equality of opportunity;
6. It does not mean absence of restraint, competition or ideology.
7. Rights are claims of the citizen against the State, recognised and enforced by it - not claims of the State against citizens
nor privileges of a few;
8. in India they are made justiciable through Part III read with Arts 32 and 226.
9. Social capital is a distinct, intangible resource - the level of mutual trust, harmony, networks and reciprocity in a society
- as opposed to physical capital (buildings, infrastructure, machines) and human capital (literacy, skills, working-age
population).
Constitutionalism and Constitutional Morality
1. Constitutionalism is the doctrine that governmental power must be limited by and exercised through law - 'limited
government'.
2. A country may possess a Constitution without having constitutionalism (authoritarian regimes have written
constitutions but unchecked power);
3. the two are therefore not the same thing.
4. Its essential ingredients are: rule of law, separation of powers with checks and balances, judicial review, enforceable
fundamental rights, an independent judiciary, free and fair periodic elections, and a government accountable to the
people.
5. Constitutional morality: a phrase Ambedkar borrowed from the historian George Grote and pressed in the Constituent
Assembly (4 November 1948).
It means following the spirit and core values of the Constitution, not mere literal legality, and the willingness of all actors
to work it with restraint.
6. Illustrations: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) - the proclamation dissolving the Bihar Assembly on the
Governor's report was held unconstitutional and mala fide;
7. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) - judicial review is part of the Basic Structure, so even Ninth Schedule laws
inserted after 24 April 1973 can be tested;
8. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) - constitutional morality prevails over popular/social morality.
Sovereignty and its Kinds
Sovereignty is the supreme, original and independent authority of the State, one of the four essential elements of a State
and the one that distinguishes a State from every other association.
KINDS OF SOVEREIGNTY
1. Internal: supremacy over all persons and associations within the territory.
2. External: freedom from foreign control in the conduct of relations with other States.
3. Legal: the authority that makes law and whose commands the courts enforce. In India the Constitution is supreme; in
Britain, Parliament.
4. Political: the electorate behind the legal sovereign, whose will ultimately prevails.
5. Popular: power flows from the people, declared in the opening words WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA and worked through
universal adult franchise.
6. De jure against de facto: legal title to rule as against actual effective control.
7. Pluralist view (Harold Laski): the State is only one association among many and not absolutely supreme.
- Parliamentary sovereignty in the United Kingdom means no court can question an Act of Parliament.
- India instead follows constitutional supremacy, so Parliament's power to legislate and to amend is limited and judicially
reviewable.

Doctrines - I: Severability, Eclipse, Colourable Legislation
1. Doctrine of Severability (Separability) - under Art 13, when only a part of a law offends the Constitution, the court
strikes down only that offending part if it can be separated from the rest;
2. If the valid and invalid parts are inseparable, the whole law falls (A.K. Gopalan, 1950, where only s.14 of the Preventive
Detention Act was voided; R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla, 1957).
3. Doctrine of Eclipse - a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is not dead but dormant;
4. The dormant law stays valid for past transactions and for people who cannot claim that right (for example, those who
are not citizens, for Art 19 rights).
When an amendment removes the conflict, it revives automatically (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P., 1955).
5. It does not apply the same way to post-Constitution laws violating Fundamental Rights, which are void from inception
(Deep Chand, 1959;
6. Mahendra Lal Jaini, 1963), though such a law may still operate against non-citizens where the right is available only to
citizens.
7. Doctrine of Colourable Legislation - 'what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly'.
8. a legislature cannot use a subject within its competence as a mere pretence to legislate on a subject outside it.
9. The test goes to legislative competence, not to the motive or bona fides of the legislature (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v.
State of Orissa, 1953).
Doctrines - II: Pith and Substance, Harmonious Construction, Territorial Nexus, Repugnancy
1. Pith and Substance - to test a law against the Seventh Schedule the court looks at its true nature and character, not its
form;
2. If in pith and substance it falls within the legislature's own List, an incidental encroachment on another List does not
invalidate it (Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee, 1947, Privy Council; F.N. Balsara, 1951).
3. Harmonious Construction - overlapping provisions or List entries must be read so as to give effect to both, and one
should not be so construed as to render the other nugatory;
4. It is used to reconcile Fundamental Rights with DPSPs (In re Kerala Education Bill, 1957; Minerva Mills, 1980).
5. Doctrine of Territorial Nexus: under Art 245(1), a State law normally applies only within that State.
A State law that operates outside the State is still valid if there is a real (not illusory) connection between the State and
the object taxed or regulated (State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala, 1957);
6. Art 245(2) protects Parliament's laws absolutely - no law of Parliament is invalid merely because it operates
extra-territorially.
7. Doctrine of Repugnancy - Art 254(1): on a Concurrent List subject, if a State law is repugnant to a Parliamentary law or
an existing law, the Union law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy;
8. Art 254(2): but if the State law was reserved for and received the President's assent, it prevails in that State - subject
to Parliament's power to later add to, amend or repeal it.
TERMS WHERE THE CONSTITUTION IS NOT CLEAR
- Not Mentioned - Federation, Judicial Review, Vice President removal, Offices of leader of house and leader of opposition
- Mentioned but not defined - Minority, Martial law, Untouchability, Cabinet - Added by 44th CAA but without defining

AMENDING PROCEDURE
1. Special Majority: Art 368(2) [PRELIMS 2024, 2022]
CONDITION
- Any amendment not covered by the proviso to Art 368(2), i.e. one that does not affect the federal provisions or the
Seventh Schedule.
- Examples: Fundamental Rights, DPSPs, and most other provisions.
MAJORITY NEEDED
- Special majority in each House: a majority of the total membership and 2/3 of members present and voting.
- Presidential assent is mandatory (24th CAA, 1971).
- The Basic Structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) limits this amending power.
2. Special Majority + State Ratification: Proviso to Art 368(2) [PRELIMS 2013]
CONDITION: the amendment affects any of the following:
1. Election of the President (Arts 54, 55);
2. Extent of the executive power of the Union and the States (Arts 73, 162);
3. The Supreme Court, the High Courts, and High Courts for UTs (Art 241);
4. Distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States, and any List in the Seventh Schedule;
5. GST Council (Art 279A, added by the 101st CAA, 2016);
6. Representation of States in Parliament;
7. Article 368 itself.
MAJORITY NEEDED
- Special majority in each House, plus ratification by the legislatures of not less than half the States, by simple
majority.

- The Constitution sets no time limit for State ratification.
- Presidential assent is required.
- The aim is to protect federalism: matters that affect the States cannot be changed by Parliament alone.
3. Simple Majority: Arts 2 and 3 (outside Art 368)
CONDITION
- Art 2: admission or establishment of new States from territory outside India.
- Art 3: formation of new States, and alteration of the areas, boundaries or names of existing States.
MAJORITY NEEDED
- Simple majority in both Houses of Parliament.

- Example (Art 3): formation of Telangana under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014.
- TRAP: Sikkim was made a State by the 36th CAA, 1975, not by a simple-majority law.
